newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's central bank chief upbeat on economy.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's central bank chief upbeat on economy.

text.p: Hungary is on the right track to further improve the performance of the economy this year and in 1997, the head of Hungary's central bank said on Wednesday.
"Hungary's economic processes are moving in the right direction," National Bank of Hungary (NBH) President Gyorgy Suranyi told a news conference.
Suranyi said Hungary was likely to reach most of its main 1996 economic policy targets, and planned to reduce its state budget further and stop the decline of real wages in 1997.
"We expect the (1996) current account deficit to remain below the $2 billion target," he said.

The NBH said in a later statement that according to preliminary figures, the current account deficit widened by $103 million dollars in August to $1,070 million, correcting a rough August deficit figure it gave earlier of $100 million.
Suranyi said the government will probably reduce its spending to 44.1 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) this year from 53.5 percent in 1995 and 58.7 percent in 1994.
"Budget expenditures and the burdens on the business sector dramatically decreased in the past two years," he said.

Suranyi predicted that the country's net foreign currency debt will decline to 38.2 percent of the GDP this year and 36.9 percent next year, compared with 38.4 percent in 1995 and 45.9 percent in the previous year.

Year-on-year inflation is likely to drop to 20 percent by December from 28.3 percent in the last month of 1995, Suranyi said. However, inflation did not decline as rapidly as the central bank expected, he added.
Finance Ministry State Secretary Csaba Laszlo told the same news conference that the country is also likely to keep its budget deficit to the original target of four percent of the GDP.
Suranyi said Hungary's GDP is seen growing by two to three percent next year, compared to forecast of two percent in 1996.
He added the decline of real wages is likely to slow down later this year and will stop or be reversed in 1997.
"We estimate that this will drop to two or three percent by the end of this year," Suranyi said. "Nobody expects further decline for next year, and we cannot exclude a modest rise."

According to figures published on Tuesday by the Central Statistical Office, average monthly incomes were 4.5 percent lower in real terms in the January-August period than in the same period of last year.
